source.title: NegVQA: Can Vision Language Models Understand Negation?
source.authors: Yuhui Zhang; Yu-Chang Su; Yiming Liu; S. Yeung-Levy

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests how model scale relates to downstream task accuracy in vision-language models, a different modality and task from language-model held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates VLM accuracy on negated and non-negated questions and reports qualitative scaling trends. It does not test held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation from fitted small runs, or compute-optimal allocation. The appendix table is flattened in the supplied text, so values other than the explicitly stated Qwen2-VL-72B accuracies are not assigned to individual models.
record.test_reason: The study compares zero-shot VQA accuracy across model sizes within seven VLM families. That is a new-setting result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It fits no scaling law and measures no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that VLMs struggle substantially with negation (an average drop of 29.7 points) and report 'a hint' of U-shaped scaling on NegVQA. They attribute it to steadily improving base QA combined with a tanh-like onset of negation understanding.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates zero-shot VLM accuracy on a negated visual-question-answering benchmark; it does not fit language-model pretraining-loss or compute-allocation scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling pattern differs by question condition: original questions show a positive trend, while negated questions show a U-shaped trend, especially in reasoning and document/chart categories.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evaluation is zero-shot and multiple-choice; the authors note that this may not represent open-ended or real-world negation handling, and few-shot effects are not tested. The reported scaling trends are qualitative here, and flattened table values prevent reliable assignment of most individual model accuracies and confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model/category numerical accuracies and confidence intervals from Appendix Table 1 were not extracted because the supplied table is flattened and the values cannot be reliably matched to its columns. No other separately stated claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: Whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss, any fitted functional form or extrapolation, and scaling in tokens or compute (only parameter count is varied, observationally across released models).

missing.what: Per-family NegVQA trends that are not U-shaped. Qwen2-VL rises monotonically (about 53.4 → 57.2 → 72.7), as do Molmo (about 30 → 37 → 56 → 75) and InstructBLIP (28.9 → 35.2). LLaVA-1.5 declines (47.9 → 40.3). These are needed to tell which families show U-shaped, monotonic or inverse scaling.
Per-dataset scaling curves for the 20 source datasets, on both PosVQA and NegVQA.

record.verdict_notes: The record's labels were broadly right. I removed R1 and R2 from V6 because single-model results carry no scale information, and added per-family missing data. Scale here is parameter count across independently trained released models with different data, so size is confounded with training recipe. The U-shape claim is qualitative. Table values were read from flattened text and should be verified.

versions.untested_parts: Tests scale-related accuracy trends on VQA, including negated questions; does not test pretraining-loss predictability or other downstream tasks.
